subject: Mathematics
distinctive: A mathematics EE usually takes one of two approaches. A theoretical essay explores a problem or area of mathematics outside the syllabus that made you curious, in class or in your own reading. A practical essay uses mathematics to investigate an issue you care about. The issue could come from your career plans, a CAS project, a hobby or another subject. Many essays mix both approaches.

If you have an interest that produces data, such as a sport, you can analyse that data (probably with statistics) to answer your research question. If your issue comes from another subject, the guide suggests you think about the interdisciplinary pathway. Whichever approach you take, your mathematics essay must include a review of the literature (secondary research).

The guide calls knowledge and understanding "arguably the most important criterion in a mathematics essay". You don't have to discover something new. You either explain mathematics that is new to you, or you apply mathematics you understand well to a new situation. Algebra takes up space on the page, so your final word count will probably be under 4,000 words.

sources.primary: Mathematics has no primary sources in the usual sense. In a practical essay, you start from data you collect yourself. Use raw data: data that has already been processed (for example, batting averages in baseball) leaves you little to do.
sources.secondary: Every mathematics essay must include a review of the literature. In a theoretical essay, your research is mostly reading around the subject. Choose a few of the most relevant resources, because too many sources can be confusing.

methods: Theoretical essays: read around the area of mathematics, then explain the concepts clearly and prove your ideas. The guide's examples on RSA encryption and infinite sets work this way.
Practical essays: collect suitable data and graph the data first. Only then decide which techniques to use to analyse the data.
Modelling a real situation: for example, building a population or habitat model and using the model to make a prediction.
Applying an algorithm to a real problem: for example, using an algorithm such as Dijkstra's to choose a route.
Statistical analysis of data from an interest such as sport: for example, testing whether home advantage is significant.
choosing_topic: Start from an interest: a branch of mathematics that made you curious, or an issue from your career plans, a CAS project, a hobby or another subject that mathematics could investigate.

Narrow your interest to a topic. In a theoretical essay, the topic can name the area of mathematics you'll explore. In a practical essay, the topic can show how mathematics will explore your area of interest.
Once your topic is narrow and focused, write a first version of your research question. Expect the wording of your research question to change a little as your research goes on.

Be careful with research questions that compare two approaches. The guide says a comparison of RSA with elliptic curves couldn't be explained fully in 4,000 words, so a question on RSA alone is better.
In a practical essay, don't name the mathematics or statistical methods in your research question. Your choice of method may change once you look at your data.
Don't be too ambitious. You don't need mathematics beyond the syllabus: you may be able to answer your research question with the mathematics you've already studied.

examples.rq: What is RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) encryption and how does it help make the internet secure?
examples.why: A mainly theoretical essay. You explain how RSA works, showing full understanding of any mathematics beyond the syllabus. Then you explain how RSA keeps online transactions secure. The guide prefers this one-method question to a comparison of RSA with elliptic curves.

A mainly theoretical essay. You explore countably infinite sets, explain the concepts clearly and prove your ideas. Then you move on to the uncountable continuum and discuss how the idea of infinity could be extended further.

examples.rq: What are fractals and what is fractal dimension? (or: Length of a coastline)
examples.why: A mainly theoretical essay. You explain how fractals develop and why fractals matter. You might explore limits problems, such as a finite area with an infinite perimeter. From there, you could move on to the length of the coastline of a favourite island, or to fractal dimension.

examples.rq: How long do the rhinos have left?
examples.why: A mainly practical essay. You explore both the population size and the habitat of the rhinoceros. You try to build a realistic model for the population or the habitat area, and use the model to predict which one reaches zero first. The guide says you would start by graphing the data.

examples.topic: Getting to school by public transport
examples.rq: What is the quickest and/or cheapest route from your home to school?
examples.why: A mainly practical essay. You study the transport system in your area and compare different ways of getting to school. You estimate travel and walking times, then use an algorithm such as Dijkstra's to choose your preferred route.

examples.topic: Winning the English football Premier League
examples.rq: What is “home advantage”, and are Premier League football champions equally successful away from home?
examples.why: A mainly practical essay. You use raw Premier League results to look at how goals scored at home and away are distributed. You test whether home advantage is significant, and check whether the champions overcome home advantage in away games. The guide says you would start by graphing the data.

structure: Introduction: explain your research question and your plan clearly, in your own words. Start from mathematics you know from the syllabus.
Show and explain every essential step in your own words. Subheadings may help, depending on the mathematics you explore.
If the proof of a complicated theorem is too difficult, you may quote the theorem without proving it. You must still explain what the theorem is for and give an example of the theorem in use.
In a practical essay, explain the background, then show your data before your analysis. Put large amounts of data in an appendix.
Write your mathematics with an equation editor. Use a new line for each step of algebra, and never use * for multiplication or ^ for powers.
pitfalls: Including mathematics you don't fully understand. If you can't explain the mathematics, leave it out and change your plan.
Relying too much on your sources, or copying information straight from your sources.
Trying to fit in too much (two methods, for example), so your understanding of the mathematics no longer shows clearly.
Working with processed data instead of raw data.
Choosing your analysis techniques before you've looked at your data.
Taking your analysis beyond your research question. The guide says extra analysis is likely to weaken your essay.
rules: Every mathematics essay must include a review of the literature (secondary research).
In a data-based essay, use raw data, not data that has already been processed.
think: Can you name the specific area of mathematics, or the specific data set, your essay would be built on?
Could you explain your mathematics step by step, in your own words, starting from what you know from the syllabus?
If your idea compares two methods, could you show full understanding of both methods in 4,000 words? Or should you focus on one method?
If your essay is practical, can you get raw data, not figures someone has already processed?
Does your research question leave the choice of mathematical or statistical method open until you've graphed your data?
Is your question mainly about mathematics, or would the question fit better in another subject or the interdisciplinary pathway?

subject: Visual Arts
distinctive: In a visual arts EE, you explore a topic that interests you in visual arts. Your essay must combine analysis of primary sources (your chosen artworks) with careful research that uses scholarly methods. Then you critically evaluate the results. Secondary sources such as books, critiques, magazine articles, interviews, subject journals and websites must support your argument as evidence.

Your chosen artworks are your body of work. Your body of work needs enough substance for an in-depth 4,000-word essay. The guide doesn't set an exact number. Start by looking for works that go well together, for example three or four by the same artist. As you analyse the works, you may find that three are enough to compare and contrast, or that a fourth adds depth to your analysis.

Arts essays more often use qualitative research methods, which aim to understand the art form in its context. Approaches include studying aesthetic concepts, historical, social and cultural aspects, and gender-based or post-colonialist readings. The guide also sees your EE as a chance to study art in an international context, exploring both the familiar and the new.

sources.primary: In visual arts, your primary sources are the artworks you analyse. Together, your chosen artworks form your body of work. If you can't see an artwork in person, use high-quality reproductions, videos and images instead.
sources.secondary: Secondary sources such as books, critiques, magazine articles, interviews, subject journals and websites must be used as evidence for your argument. Secondary sources give context, support the points in your analysis and explain the circumstances behind an artist's decisions. The views of artists, curators, historians and critics can add different perspectives.

methods: Artistic and contextual analysis of your chosen artworks: look at what the artworks say and also how the artworks say it.
Qualitative research that tries to understand the art form in its context. Your essay must show clear knowledge and understanding of at least one suitable context.
Readings through aesthetic concepts, through historical, social and cultural aspects, or through gender-based and post-colonialist lenses.
Comparing two or more artworks. Your comparisons must be valid and come from sensitive, objective analysis. Each comparison needs a clear, significant purpose that you explain.
For an influence topic: rigorous formal analysis (analysis of the visual elements of the works), backed by documents that give evidence of the influence.
choosing_topic: Keep your topic inside visual arts. The arts link to many other subjects, but the guide warns against topics that sit at the edge of the arts subject.
You must answer your research question through artistic and contextual analysis. Your essay must not drift into subjects such as psychology, history or sociology.

You may discuss a social, political or gender issue that comes from an artwork. Focus on the artistic meaning and significance of the artwork. Don't use the artwork only as documentary evidence of the issue.

Think carefully before writing about one artist's or style's influence on another. Finding similarities is fairly easy. Showing an actual influence is hard, and needs formal analysis plus documentary evidence.
Read the existing literature on your topic. The literature helps you build your research question and judge whether your research question is relevant.
Choose a limited number of artworks: enough substance to keep making new points without repeating yourself, and few enough to analyse in depth within the word limit.

examples.topic: The influence of Japanese prints on Claude Monet’s artistic practice
examples.rq: To what extent did aesthetic principles of Japanese prints from the Edo period influence Claude Monet’s material and conceptual artistic practice?
examples.why: The guide names this as a good approach to an influence topic. You research the features of Edo-period Japanese prints and of Impressionist paintings. Then you analyse Monet artworks from one period of his life after another, to trace how his ideas and his use of materials developed. You look for secondary sources that give evidence of the influence, and give examples to support your claims. Finally, you evaluate the strengths and limitations of your research and conclude on how far the influence went.

examples.topic: The embodiment of the cyclical nature of life and death in work by Joni Brenner
examples.rq: To what extent does the Skull Series of compositions by Joni Brenner embody the cyclical nature of life and death?
examples.why: You first research the social and historical context of Apartheid in South Africa and of post-Apartheid art, so that you understand Brenner's ideas and subjects. Then you analyse the artistic and symbolic features of the Skull Series and judge how far the artworks embody the cycle of life and death. You illustrate your points, evaluate the strengths and limitations of your research, and conclude on how far the Skull Series embodies that cycle.

structure: Images are required in a visual arts essay and must appear in the body of the essay. Choose images carefully, to help the reader understand your essay.
Identify and cite every image, both in the essay itself and in the separate list of sources at the end. Every image must be a reasonable size and in high-quality resolution.
Build your argument from artworks you've analysed and explained, supported by secondary sources. The guide says combining both gives the most convincing argument.
Support each point with examples from the artworks you examine. Use artistic terms and concepts fluently and accurately.

In your discussion, point the reader to evidence in the artworks and in your secondary research, in a balanced way. Identify the strengths and limitations of your research, and how those strengths and limitations shaped your interpretation and conclusions.
pitfalls: Choosing a topic at the edge of visual arts, so that your essay turns into psychology, history or sociology.
Treating an artwork only as documentary evidence for a social, political or gender issue.
Claiming that one artist influenced another because their works look similar, without formal analysis and supporting documents.
Building your argument mainly by quoting or summarising secondary sources. The guide says an argument built that way is likely to be limited.
Choosing too few artworks (so you overanalyse or repeat points), or too many to analyse in depth within the word limit.
Comparing artworks without explaining why the comparison matters, or making comparisons that aren't valid.
rules: Your essay must answer your research question using artistic and contextual analysis.
Secondary sources must be used as evidence for your argument. You must critically examine both your primary and your secondary sources.
Images are required in a visual arts essay and must appear in the body of the essay.
Every image must be properly identified and cited in the essay and in the list of sources, at a reasonable size and in high-quality resolution.
think: Which artworks would make up your body of work? Do those artworks give you enough to discuss for 4,000 words without repeating yourself?
Is your research question about the artistic meaning and significance of the artworks? Or is the question really about psychology, history or sociology, and just happens to involve art?
If your idea centres on a social, political or gender issue, would you analyse the artworks as art, or use the artworks only as evidence of the issue?
If you want to argue that one artist influenced another, what letters, diaries, interviews or media articles could show the influence, beyond visual similarities?
Which context would you use to read your artworks: aesthetic, historical, social, cultural, gender-based or post-colonialist?
Can you see the artworks in person? If not, can you find high-quality reproductions to put in the body of your essay?
